Hey guys, might have made one of the fastest frontend frameworks till date over the past two weeks! Firstly, Next.js pages are just JavaScript that returns HTML. So why do you need 300MB of dependencies to serve one? That bugged me. After nanobrew (1.2MB replacing 57MB Homebrew) and mcp-zig (131KB replacing 52MB of TypeScript), I couldn't not try the obvious next thing. So I built merjs. A Next.js-style web framework written entirely in Zig. Zero node_modules. 2MB binary. Ships to Cloudflare Workers. https://merlionjs.com (it's a 5kB page) Here's what routing looks like: ``` app/index.zig / app/weather.zig /weather api/ai.zig /api/ai ``` Drop a .zig file. Export render(). Run one command. Route is live. No config files. No webpack. No "oh you need to install these 17 peer dependencies first." I also built Claude Code skills for it. View them here: https://lnkd.in/grCjyHjY So you can just type `/new-page dashboard` or `/new-api users` or `/deploy` and it scaffolds the whole thing for you. Pages, API routes, WASM modules, dev server, full deploy. You don't even need to know Zig to get started. Just tell Claude what you want. The demo is a real Singapore government data dashboard. Live weather, air quality, UV index, all pulled from data.gov.sg . Not a todo app. A real thing running on Cloudflare Workers right now. https://lnkd.in/gsGsdrKm The deeper bet here is that WebAssembly breaks the last reason Node.js owned the server. JS won because it ran in the browser. Now Zig can too. Write your server in Zig, compile client logic to .wasm, ship it. No bundler. No hydration. One language, two targets. 2MB binary. 2,400+ req/s. Zero node_modules. Built in Singapore. Still very experimental but it works. If you've ever looked at your node_modules folder and thought "this can't be right," I'd love to hear from you. https://lnkd.in/gbrjp4MG powered by OpenAIDevs 's codex assisted with the build too! → https://merlionjs.com → https://lnkd.in/gtF2q7UQ #zig #webdev #wasm #cloudflare #singapore #opensource #buildinpublic ...more ...more

Someone found a faster algorithm than Dijkstra's after 69 years. And that's absolutely wild. Time to drop some graph theory lore. Dijkstra invented his single-source shortest-path algorithm in 1956, and it is remarkable for how long it has stood as the best deterministic algorithm for this problem. Since then, the only improvements have come from tweaking the priority queue, culminating with Fibonacci heaps in the 1980's, yielding a runtime of O(E + V log V) (if you want to review Dijkstra's algorithm, see https://lnkd.in/gGhsmuJJ ). And then, out of nowhere, a new 2025 paper, "Breaking the Sorting Barrier for Directed Single-Source Shortest Paths" (by Ran Duan, Jiayi Mao, Xiao Mao, Xinkai Shu, and Longhui Yin) comes out with a new O(E * (log V)^0.67)-time algorithm. This beats Dijkstra for sparse graphs. To see how crazy that is, compare it with the table below, which shows the slow, gradual improvements for another classic graph problem: the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) problem. Dijkstra's reign lasted so long that it was widely believed to be optimal. In fact, if I read between the lines, it seems that the legendary Robert E Tarjan (co-inventor of the Fibonacci heap mentioned above, and who is all over the MST table below) has recently been trying to prove that Dijkstra's algorithm is truly optimal. Two of his most recent papers, "Bidirectional Dijkstra's Algorithm is Instance-Optimal" (2024) and "Universal Optimality of Dijkstra via Beyond-Worst-Case Heaps" (2023), chip away at showing how Dijkstra is optimal in different aspects, almost--but not quite--precluding the new result! 1956-2025. What a run. ...more ...more

While early graduation was never a deliberate goal, it has been the outcome of continuous learning, collaboration, and seizing opportunities along the way. I believe in celebrating achievements—not for self-promotion, but as a testament to the effort, growth, and collective impact of this journey. I am deeply grateful to my mentors, peers, and the opportunities that have supported me along the way. LLMs compress the entire internet into billions of parameters. Why don't we do something similar for new knowledge 🤔? Effectively storing and retrieving the desired new knowledge, without losing relationships between multiple chunks, are just some of the key challenges that we tackle in MeMo 🎯 ! To do so, we designed our data synthesis and inference pipeline around a single guiding principle: reflections 💭 . Check out how we compare against State of the Art RAG-based methods (e.g. NV-Embed-V2, HippoRAG2, etc...) in what my co-author Arun Verma has written. ❗ Spoiler: MeMo might just be what you need when answers span multiple chunks in complex multi-hop or long-context-understanding tasks. As a step towards building Continual Learning capabilities for AI system, I am grateful to have this joint work with my co-authors 🙏 - Simon Lee , Alfred Leong , Arun Verma , Alok Prakash , Nancy Chen , Bryan Kian Hsiang Low , Daniela Rus , and Armando Solar-Lezama 📄 Paper: https://lnkd.in/gtMKG6mF 🌐 Blog page: https://lnkd.in/gjNmrm25 #LLM #ContinualLearning #KnowledgeIntegration #MemoryAugmentedAI #RAG #NLP #AI #AIMemory
